doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Learning on the road, Adelstein, and meeting Bobby Shew
summary: Why he chose the road over classical playing, Bernard Adelstein reluctantly teaching him at home, and Bobby Shew hearing him open for Woody Herman.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well you can’t learn that, I don’t think they teach that in jazz education now, maybe there’s not a reason for it, but I’m envious that you had that experience and that down the road some of the things you did you say well this is easy compared to being in the pit.

Oh absolutely. But once again I’m getting back to, it was fun you know, it was fun you know? Music should be fun. It should not be — well that’s why I chose not to be a classical player. I didn’t want to sit there and count a hundred bars and then come in. I wanted to play my horn. And that’s why every night I’d go — every night on the road I’d go to a club and play, with different players. That’s how I learned. That was the school — that was my college training, and learning how to play from different players all over the country. And all over the world for that matter. It was — that’s the way I think it should be. Of course it’s not, there’s no opportunity for that anymore. You have college bands which are wonderful, you have North Texas, you’ve got — oh there’s so many — Indiana, I’m sure your school is fantastic, Florida — there’s a lot of places. I had a choice you know except our family was very poor and I got a full scholarship to the Cleveland Institute of Music. So, and I wanted to study with Bernard Adelstein. And Bernard was the class — he was the principal trumpet player with Cleveland. And I would do gigs with him in Cleveland, commercials, jingles, and I’d play first he’d play third. You know so we were good friends. So when I went on the road and I came out I had a full scholarship, he didn’t know this and I came there to the school to study with him. And he said, “What are you doing here?” I said, “I’m here to study with you.” He says, “No you’re not, you go back on the road.” Because he knew that’s what I wanted to do. And it was very hard and I said, “No. I want to study with you. I want to learn from you what I can.” And finally he gave in and said, “Okay but only if you come to my house and study with me at my house.” Because he had all postgraduate students except me. I was the only one, an outsider. And these postgraduate students, I’d hear them play [scats] all over the place and I’m going oh my goodness, I can’t do that you know. So he took me in, in his house, and I — it was great. Fantastic you know. So I learned from him and then he knew like I wanted to go back on the road and then I did, I went back on the road right away, with the Jimmy Dorsey band again, and then I got heard. I was in Cleveland playing in an R&B band and we opened for Woody Herman’s band. And on Woody Herman’s band was Bobby Shew. And that’s when Bill Chase was playing. Bill was like the star of the Woody Herman band. But Shew was in the trumpet section. And I knew Bob, because he was on the road — I met Bobby when I was 12 or something like that.
